properties.name: Strait of Hormuz
properties.current_situation: Functional closure since 2-3 March 2026, still in force in mid-August. Traffic in the week to 9 August 2026: 78 transits, of which 45 were not Iranian-linked, down from 95 the week before — heavily reduced but no longer near-zero. Brent stood at $88.59, well below the $126 peak of March. The IEA's record 400M-barrel stock release, demand destruction across South and Southeast Asia, and rerouting have absorbed much of the shock. Iran conditions reopening on the release of frozen assets and an end to regional conflicts including Lebanon.
properties.key_dependents: China, India, Japan, South Korea (69% of all flows). Singapore (45% of LNG). Philippines, Thailand, Bangladesh, Pakistan — all in active energy crisis.
properties.alternative_routes: Saudi East-West Pipeline (~4 mb/d). UAE ADCOP/Fujairah Pipeline (~1.8 mb/d). Combined bypass covers <45% of normal flow — 55%+ of volumes stranded.
properties.economic_impact: Brent peaked at $126 in March 2026 and was $88.59 in August — the price shock has largely unwound while the physical closure has not. Roughly $1.5-2bn in insurance claims from about 70 casualties since late February. Multiple Asian countries remain under energy emergency measures, and LNG carrier spot rates have softened on oversupply.
properties.historical: 1984-88 Tanker War: 546 vessels attacked, 430+ seafarers killed, but oil kept flowing. 2026 is fundamentally different — first functional complete closure. No modern precedent for a 20% supply shock.
properties.one_line: 21 miles wide, 20% of global oil and LNG. Closed since early March 2026 — but Brent is back to $88 and the world adapted faster than the strait reopened.

sources.note: 78 transits week to 9 Aug 2026; 45 non-Iranian; ~$1.5-2bn claims

properties.name: Bab el-Mandeb
properties.current_situation: Houthi attacks began November 2023: 178+ vessels hit, four ships sunk, nine sailors killed, container traffic down 90% at peak. The October 2025 Gaza ceasefire triggered a Houthi ceasefire; the last vessel attack was on 29 September 2025 and the Houthis declared an end to attacks 43 days later. Carriers have returned only cautiously — Maersk's first transit since early 2024 came in December 2025, and CMA CGM restored its MEDEX and INDAMEX services from January 2026. The security problem was solved well before the traffic problem.
properties.key_dependents: Europe (most penalized — disrupted Asia-Europe trade). Qatar (30M tonnes/year LNG fully dependent on this route). China, India (container exports). Egypt (Suez revenue collapsed from $10.2B to $4.1B).
properties.alternative_routes: Cape of Good Hope: +11,000 nautical miles, +10 days transit, +$1M fuel per voyage, +$200-400/TEU. Freight rates up 25-35% above pre-crisis.
properties.economic_impact: ~$1 trillion in goods disrupted (Oct 2023-May 2024). 25% of global container trade affected. Insurance premiums spiked for Red Sea transit. Suez Canal revenue cut by 60%.
properties.historical: Historically a piracy zone but never blocked at this scale. Houthi campaign is the first time a non-state actor effectively closed a major global shipping lane for over a year.
properties.one_line: 16 miles wide, 12% of global trade. The Houthis stopped attacking in late 2025 — and a hundred days later the ships still had not come back.

sources.note: 100 days since the last attack; traffic still ~60% down

properties.name: Suez Canal
properties.current_situation: Downstream casualty of the Bab el-Mandeb crisis. In the first week of 2026, transits were still about 60% below the equivalent week of 2023 — despite 100 days without an attack. Revenue fell from $10.2B (2023) to $4.1B (2025), the lowest in roughly a decade in nominal terms. Recovery through 2026 has been partial: carriers returned selectively from January, and by August traffic was broadly unchanged with an uptick in VLCC movements as tanker operators rerouted. Rerouting decisions, once made, are slow to reverse.
properties.key_dependents: Egypt (revenue-dependent: canal is 5-8% of GDP). Europe-Asia trade corridor. CMA CGM, Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd (major shipping lines). 12% of global trade normally flows through.
properties.alternative_routes: Cape of Good Hope: same penalty as Bab el-Mandeb reroute since they're sequential. +10-14 days, +$1M fuel. No other alternative exists for Asia-Europe shipping.
properties.economic_impact: Egypt lost ~$6B in annual revenue. Shanghai-to-Europe container rates spiked 256% (Dec 2023-Feb 2024). 2025 average still 80% above pre-crisis. War-risk surcharge: $200-800/container.
properties.historical: Ever Given blockage (March 2021): 6 days, 300+ vessels blocked, $92.7B cargo affected, $136.9B total industry losses. 1956 and 1967: canal closed during wars. 1967-1975: closed 8 years during Arab-Israeli conflict.
properties.one_line: 300 metres wide, 12% of global trade. Traffic was still 60% below 2023 a hundred days after the attacks stopped. Restoring safety did not restore the route.

sources.note: Transits ~60% below 2023 despite 100 days without attack

properties.name: Panama Canal
properties.current_situation: Recovered from the 2023-24 drought: Gatún Lake refilled to near capacity and reached 87.7 feet in July 2026. FY2025 revenue rose 14.4% to $5.7B on 13,404 transits, up 19.3%, with daily averages back to 33 from 27 during the drought. As of early August 2026 the canal was running 36 daily slots. But an El Niño warning has driven successive draft cuts at the Neopanamax locks: 49.5 feet from 3 July 2026, 49.0 feet from 24 July, and 48.5 feet expected from 15 August. The constraint is rainfall, and it is returning.
properties.key_dependents: United States (40% of US container traffic, 72.5% of all canal traffic in FY2021). China (13-22% of traffic). LNG trade: Atlantic-to-Pacific. Grain exports: US Gulf to Asia.
properties.alternative_routes: Suez Canal (+10-14 days for Asia traffic). Cape Horn for South America. No overnight LNG transits allowed — limited slots even when operating. New Indio River dam approved January 2025; gas pipeline/land bridge in pre-qualification (April 2025).
properties.economic_impact: FY2025 revenue $5.7B, up 14.4%. Capacity restored to 36 daily slots against 22-24 at the depth of the drought. The renewed draft restrictions reduce cargo per transit rather than transit count, so the cost lands on shippers as lightering and split loads. Climate variability, not geopolitics, remains this chokepoint's binding constraint.
properties.historical: Opened 1914. Expanded 2016 (neo-Panamax locks). 2023-24 drought was worst in canal's 110-year history. Unlike other chokepoints, the threat is hydrological, not geopolitical.
properties.one_line: 150 metres wide, 5% of global trade. The drought ended and the canal came back — then an El Niño warning started cutting the draft again, a foot at a time.

sources.note: Draft cuts: 49.5ft from 3 Jul, 49.0ft from 24 Jul, 48.5ft expected 15 Aug 2026

properties.name: Strait of Malacca
properties.current_situation: As of mid-2025, not re-verified in the August 2026 refresh: World's busiest strait: 258 ships/day average, 94,301 transits in 2024 (+5.5% YoY). 23.2M barrels/day oil in first half 2025 (22% of global, 29% of seaborne). Piracy surging: 80 incidents in first half 2025 vs 21 in all of 2024 — 380% increase. China-US naval tension escalating. Phillips Channel narrows to 2.8km near Singapore.
properties.key_dependents: China (80% of crude imports). Japan (90% of oil imports). South Korea (80% of oil imports). Singapore (refining/transshipment hub). $3.5 trillion in annual trade value.
properties.alternative_routes: Sunda Strait (shallow, strong currents). Lombok/Makassar Strait (longer, more expensive). China-Myanmar pipeline (operational 2013, limited capacity). Thailand canal proposals (not built). All alternatives are inferior.
properties.economic_impact: Not currently disrupted in trade-flow terms — but piracy costs, insurance premiums, and naval posturing are rising. The 'Malacca Dilemma' is entrenched in Chinese strategic doctrine. A blockade scenario would dwarf Hormuz in scale.
properties.historical: Historical piracy zone for centuries. Modern piracy peaked 2000-2006 before coordinated patrols. Current surge (2024-2025) is the worst in over a decade. Geopolitically, it's the chokepoint most likely to become a flashpoint in US-China competition.
properties.one_line: 1.7 miles wide at Phillips Channel, 30% of global trade, 258 ships/day. Not blocked — but piracy surging 380% and it's ground zero for US-China naval tension.
